title: A Brief Reprieve and Jeremiah Imprisoned
summary: Zedekiah, the king Babylon put on Judah's throne, sends to Jeremiah asking for prayer when an Egyptian army forces the Babylonians to lift their siege of Jerusalem. Jeremiah answers that the Egyptians will go home and the Babylonians will return and burn the city. When Jeremiah tries to leave for his home territory during the lull, he is arrested as a deserter, beaten, and jailed; the king consults him in secret and then moves him to the courtyard of the guard.
story: Chapter 36 took place in the days of Jehoiakim; this chapter jumps ahead to the last reign in Judah, about 588 BC, when the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem is under way. Verses 1 and 2 give the verdict on the whole reign before the story starts: neither king, officials, nor people listened. What follows shows how that refusal looked day by day. Zedekiah wants the prophet's prayers but not his message, and he treats the Egyptian advance as a sign that the danger has passed. From here until the city falls in chapter 39, Jeremiah is a prisoner, and the narrative follows him from cell to courtyard to cistern.
historical:
After Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 597 BC and deported King Jehoiachin (called Coniah in verse 1), he installed Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as king and renamed him Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). Zedekiah later rebelled, and the Babylonian army returned and began the siege in the ninth year of his reign, about January 588 BC (39:1). The "Pharaoh" of verse 5 is almost certainly Hophra (called Apries by the Greek historians), who is named in 44:30. An Egyptian force marched into the region, and the Babylonians temporarily lifted the siege to deal with it. That reprieve is the setting of this chapter.

The Lachish letters, ostraca (inscribed pottery fragments) found in 1935 at the site of Lachish, southwest of Jerusalem, come from these same months. One of them (Letter 3) reports that a Judean commander named Konyahu son of Elnathan had gone down to Egypt, which fits the picture of Judah seeking Egyptian help. Two figures named here may also appear on clay seal impressions found in the City of David by Eilat Mazar: in 2005 a bulla belonging to Jehucal son of Shelemiah (verse 3), and in 2008 one belonging to Gedaliah son of Pashhur (38:1). Many scholars accept these as the same officials; others urge caution, since such names were not rare.
cultural:
When a king sent a delegation to a prophet asking for prayer (verse 3), he was seeking an intercessor to plead with God for the city, as Hezekiah had done with Isaiah when the Assyrians threatened Jerusalem (2 Kings 19). Zedekiah's request is conventional piety. The difference is that Hezekiah also believed the answer he received.

Jeremiah's hometown, Anathoth, lay a few miles northeast of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin (1:1). The phrase in verse 12 about claiming his portion is obscure in Hebrew; it may refer to a family inheritance, possibly connected with the field he buys in chapter 32, but that is uncertain. In wartime, anyone leaving a besieged city toward enemy lines was suspect, and some Judeans did go over to the Babylonians (38:19, 39:9). Ancient kingdoms had few purpose-built prisons; prisoners were held in rooms, pits, or cisterns within official houses, like the house of Jonathan the scribe (verse 15). The courtyard of the guard was a less severe confinement within the palace complex, and the daily loaf from the street of the bakers reflects a city where trades were grouped by street.
literary: The chapter has two halves that mirror each other. In each, King Zedekiah seeks a word from Jeremiah (verses 3 and 17), and in each the answer is the same: the city will fall to Babylon. Between them sits the arrest, which shows what the officials do with a prophet whose message they dislike. The dialogue is sharp and short. Irijah's accusation, "You are deserting to the Chaldeans", is met with "That is a lie" (verses 13 and 14). Jeremiah's question in verse 19, "Where are your prophets", turns the scene into a courtroom in which the absent false prophets stand accused. The chapter ends in partial relief, not rescue: bread every day, until the bread runs out.

outline.t: The king asks for prayer as Egypt approaches
The Babylonians will return and burn the city
Jeremiah arrested as a deserter and jailed
A secret interview and a move to the courtyard of the guard

doctrines.note: The movements of empires answer to God's word. Egypt's army comes and goes, and even a defeated Babylonian army of wounded men would rise and burn the city (verse 10), because the outcome has been decreed.
Zedekiah asks, "Please pray to the LORD our God for us" (verse 3), yet refuses the word that prayer receives. The chapter exposes prayer used as insurance rather than submission.
Jeremiah suffers not for wrongdoing but for faithfulness. He is falsely accused, beaten, and jailed, and he protests his innocence (verse 18) without changing his message.

words.note: Nasha, to deceive or beguile. In verse 9 the people are warned not to deceive themselves. The danger is not only false prophets outside but the wish inside to believe that the threat has passed.

Kasdim, Chaldeans. Originally a people of southern Mesopotamia, the Chaldeans supplied the dynasty that ruled Babylon from Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar onward, so in Jeremiah the word is a common name for the Babylonians and their army.

Palal, to pray, usually in the sense of interceding. The same verb appears when God tells Jeremiah not to pray for this people (7:16, 11:14, 14:11). The king's request in verse 3 comes after God has already said intercession will not turn the judgment aside.

christ: Jeremiah here is a righteous man, falsely accused of betraying his people, arrested at a city gate, beaten by officials, and questioned in secret by a ruler who knows the truth but fears to act on it. The pattern resembles the trial of Jesus, whom the Jewish leaders accused of subverting the nation and whom Pilate questioned privately while fearing the crowd. The New Testament doesn't cite this chapter as a prophecy of Christ, so the link is one of pattern, not prediction. It shows the long history of God's messengers suffering at the hands of the people they came to save, a history Jesus himself recalled when he lamented over Jerusalem for killing the prophets.
questions: Zedekiah wanted Jeremiah's prayers but not his message. What does it look like to want God's help without God's direction?
The Babylonian retreat looked like good news, and Jeremiah called it a false hope. How can we tell the difference between a real deliverance and a pause that tempts us to stop listening?
Jeremiah was accused of the one thing he was not doing. How should a person respond when faithfulness is mistaken for betrayal?
